title: Do Portuguese employers need a harassment code of conduct and training?
description: Portugal's Labor Code requires employers with seven or more workers to adopt a harassment code of conduct. What Law 73/2017 and CITE guidance expect.
shortAnswer: Yes, for most employers. Since Law 73/2017, Article 127(1)(k) of Portugal's Labor Code requires every employer with seven or more workers to adopt a code of good conduct for preventing and combating harassment at work, and Article 127(1)(l) requires disciplinary proceedings whenever the employer learns of alleged harassment. Breaching either is a serious offense. Guidance from the Comissão para a Igualdade no Trabalho e no Emprego (CITE) recommends a regular training plan for all staff within a zero tolerance policy.
keyTakeaways: Article 127(1)(k) of the Labor Code requires a code of good conduct on harassment where the company has seven or more workers; Article 127(1)(l) requires disciplinary proceedings when alleged harassment becomes known.
Breach of Article 127(1)(k) or (l) is a serious offense under Article 127(7), a classification Law 13/2023 kept in place.
Harassment itself is prohibited and is a very serious offense under Article 29, and the employer is liable for occupational disease caused by harassment (Article 283(8)).
CITE's model code recommends a specific, regular training plan on harassment and gender equality covering all staff, plus specific training for those who handle complaints.
Law 73/2017 also applies the code of conduct duty to public employers through the General Law on Public Service Employment.
regulator: Autoridade para as Condições do Trabalho (ACT), with the Comissão para a Igualdade no Trabalho e no Emprego (CITE) issuing guidance
appliesTo: Private sector employers with seven or more workers (code of conduct duty)
All private sector employers (disciplinary proceedings duty and prohibition of harassment)
Public employers under the Lei Geral do Trabalho em Funções Públicas
Managers, HR, and anyone designated to receive or investigate harassment complaints
All workers, who may be targets, witnesses, or perpetrators

sections.heading: Which law requires a harassment code of conduct in Portugal?

blocks.text: [Law 73/2017](https://files.diariodarepublica.pt/1s/2017/08/15700/0471504717.pdf) of August 16, 2017 (Lei n.º 73/2017, que reforça o quadro legislativo para a prevenção da prática de assédio) amended the Labor Code (Código do Trabalho, approved by Law 7/2009), the General Law on Public Service Employment (Lei Geral do Trabalho em Funções Públicas, LTFP), and the Labor Procedure Code. Under its Article 7, it entered into force on the first day of the second month after publication, that is, October 1, 2017.

It added two duties to the employer's list of general duties in Article 127(1) of the Labor Code. Article 127(1)(k) requires the employer to "Adotar códigos de boa conduta para a prevenção e combate ao assédio no trabalho, sempre que a empresa tenha sete ou mais trabalhadores": to adopt codes of good conduct for preventing and combating harassment at work whenever the company has seven or more workers. Article 127(1)(l) requires the employer to start disciplinary proceedings whenever it learns of alleged situations of harassment at work.

Article 127(7) makes breach of points (k) and (l) a serious (grave) offense. [Law 13/2023](https://files.diariodarepublica.pt/1s/2023/04/06600/0000200085.pdf) of April 3, 2023, the Decent Work Agenda reform, rewrote Article 127(7) and kept that classification for points (k) and (l). As at November 2026, that is the current text this page relies on.

sections.heading: What else did Law 73/2017 change that training should cover?

blocks.text: Law 73/2017 also tightened the substantive rules, and those changes are what a code of conduct and its training need to explain.

items: Article 29(1): harassment is prohibited outright, and under Article 29(4) the victim has a right to compensation.
Article 29(5): harassment is a very serious (muito grave) offense, without prejudice to any criminal liability.
Article 29(6): the complainant and the witnesses they name cannot be disciplined on the basis of statements in harassment proceedings until a final decision, unless they act with intent.
Article 283(8): the employer is responsible for repairing damage from occupational diseases resulting from harassment.
Article 331(2)(b): a sanction is presumed abusive if applied up to one year after a complaint or other exercise of rights on equality, non-discrimination, and harassment.
Article 394(2)(f): harassment by the employer or its representative, reported to the labor inspectorate, is listed as just cause for the worker to terminate the contract.

blocks.text: Article 4 of Law 73/2017 requires the Autoridade para as Condições do Trabalho (ACT) and the Inspeção-Geral de Finanças to provide dedicated email addresses for harassment complaints in the private and public sectors respectively, and to publish information on identifying, preventing, and responding to harassment.

sections.heading: Does the code of conduct duty apply to public employers?

blocks.text: Yes. Article 3 of Law 73/2017 amended Article 71(1) of the LTFP so that public employers must adopt codes of good conduct for preventing and combating harassment at work and start disciplinary proceedings when they learn of alleged harassment. The amended LTFP text does not repeat the seven worker threshold. Article 4(1)(d) of the LTFP was also amended to list harassment among the matters the Labor Code regulates for public servants. Training for public bodies is discussed on the [government sector](/industries/government-defence) industry page.

sections.heading: What does CITE guidance say a code and training program should contain?

blocks.text: The Comissão para a Igualdade no Trabalho e no Emprego (CITE) publishes a [guide to drafting a code of good conduct](https://cite.gov.pt/documents/14333/193238/Guia+para+a+elabora%25C3%25A7%25C3%25A3o+do+c%25C3%25B3digo+de+boa+conduta+para+a+preven%25C3%25A7%25C3%25A3o+e+combate+ao+ass%25C3%25A9dio+no+trabalho/395a274d-7df7-4cd8-a6a8-b917f90b19d4) (Guia para a elaboração de código de boa conduta para a prevenção e combate ao assédio no trabalho), with a model code. The guide is not binding, but it is the reference the equality body points employers to from its [harassment at work page](https://cite.gov.pt/assedio).

The model code covers the organization's commitment and responsibilities, scope (all people in professional or commercial relationships with the entity, inside or outside working hours, in person or online), the reporting contact, investigation and resolution by people with specialist knowledge, protection from retaliation, and sanctions. It frames a zero tolerance policy at three levels of prevention.

items: Primary prevention: a specific information strategy, and "a conceção e implementação de um plano de formação específico e regular" on sexual and moral harassment and gender equality at work, which should include all workers and collaborators, top-down.

Secondary prevention: an autonomous reporting and resolution mechanism; the people who receive and handle complaints should have specific training; anonymity, equal treatment, and non-retaliation must be guaranteed.
Tertiary prevention: a clear internal sanctions framework and, where the entity's statutes allow, support for targets who go to civil or criminal courts.

blocks.text: The guide also recommends that the commitment be attached to new contracts, that understanding of it be used as a quality indicator, and that its content be defined with the participation of workers in entities with up to 50 staff and with workers' representatives in entities with more than 250.

blocks.text: For how to fit harassment training into the wider plan, see [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix). Harassment and equality modules are also a natural part of the annual training hours covered in [Portugal's Labor Code continuous training](/regulations/portugal-labour-code-continuous-training), where that regime's conditions are met.

sections.heading: What about employers with fewer than seven workers?

blocks.text: Employers below the threshold are not required to adopt a written code, but the prohibition of harassment in Article 29, the duty to open disciplinary proceedings in Article 127(1)(l), and the employer's liability for harassment related occupational disease in Article 283(8) apply regardless of size. The employer's general duty to ensure workers' safety and health also applies; see [Portugal's OHS training requirements](/regulations/portugal-ohs-training-requirements). A short written policy and a briefing on how to raise a concern are proportionate steps even where the code is not mandatory.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry turns the code of conduct into defined concepts, such as moral and sexual harassment, reporting routes, and protection of witnesses, and links each to the roles that need it and the evidence of understanding. Mandatory Labor Code items and CITE recommendations stay labelled separately, so the program shows what the law requires and what is good practice.

faqs.q: Is harassment training itself mandatory in Portugal?
faqs.a: The Labor Code mandates the code of conduct and disciplinary proceedings, not a training course. CITE's model code recommends a specific and regular training plan for all staff and specific training for complaint handlers. In practice a code nobody has been trained on is hard to defend before the labor inspectorate.

faqs.q: How are the seven workers counted?
faqs.a: Article 127(1)(k) refers to the company having seven or more workers. The Labor Code text does not add a special counting rule, so employers should count workers under employment contracts with the company and keep the code in place if headcount fluctuates around the threshold.

faqs.q: Where can a worker in Portugal complain about harassment outside the company?
faqs.a: Article 4 of Law 73/2017 requires the ACT, for the private sector, and the Inspeção-Geral de Finanças, for the public sector, to provide dedicated email addresses for harassment complaints and to publish information about preventing and responding to harassment.

faqs.q: What does harassment cost an employer beyond fines?
faqs.a: The victim has a right to compensation under Article 29(4), the employer is responsible for repairing occupational disease caused by harassment under Article 283(8), and reported harassment by the employer is listed as just cause for the worker to resign under Article 394(2)(f).
